reviews.review: If you like tactical combat games where you rely on your decision making and synergies between characters, look elsewhere, I had previously rated this game as recommended, but I feel like I need to update it to not recommended as I've gotten farther, and here's why: The game is horrendously punishing for things far outside of your control. The elements that make it fun in the beginning like RNG and permadeath become its downfall later in the game. Strategy games are meant to reward you for thinking through situations, preparing for them adequately, and responding to changes properly. This game throws all that out the window with the power scaling differential: your adventurers start the game as weak little peasants, you spend thousands of golds to raise them up, and then by the end they're about twice as powerful as they were when they started: damage per hit, max hp, dodge, it all seems to scale at 2x. Eventually you get to the point where you can only send your people on Champion adventures, where the enemies will one shot anyone but a full tank Man-At-Arms, which seems to be the only viable playstyle. Mind you, this is my experience with the game on the EASIEST DIFFICULTY SETTING. The problem is that you invest literal hours into earning the gold and xp to level these guys up, just for them to get power lawed into the graveyard by some bad RNG. And now with one of your guys dead, your team composition is entirely destroyed, meaning the run is over. The game entirely disreg

Revising my review since I found the game a lot more fun when I replayed it, but yeah it's still bad. The developers of Darkest Dungeon do not know how to carefully craft a game. Unfortunately most of this game's difficulty comes from RNG and the fact that it punishes you by forcing you to grind. There's a lot of unnecessary time wasting in this game, too. You can ignore most of the game's mechanics if you focus on stuns and stall the game long enough to full heal your party every encounter. Besides that, getting hit with crits is pretty much the only way you can realistically lose in this game. I also think it's a huge flaw overall that multiple of the same hero can go on an expedition. It cheapens the role of each class. The game doesn't feel very intricately designed from a mechanical perspective either. There's a learning curve and then besides that it's just finding the most meta strategy and hoping your luck is fairly decent. The DLCs are much better than the base game, but that's not saying much when they both have the exact same problems. Overall I like this game for its art direction a lot, but the gameplay shouldn't be balanced around crits and accuracy as much as it is. Stress is also just a terrible mechanic. It does nothing but waste your resources at the end of every quest and make fights longer if you have to stress heal your allies. The bosses are also way too easy/straightforward. Pile on damage and 1 shot the boss. That's all it really takes. Half of the bos

To make a long story short. I just found this game tedious and frustrating to play, and I didn't feel like I was having fun or that the gameplay loop was good. The pacing felt slow and things started feeling repetitive. I quit with a team doing champ dungeons. I think this game has a problem where experimentation is punished, but you need lots of game knowledge to play optimally and the game is very deep, so I would find myself looking up the wiki page for a boss so I better understood how to make a team to beat them, because doing an entire expedition just to realize my team wasn't capable of beating the boss is just too tedious. People might say "You can't leave a bad review for Darkest dungeon just because it's too hard", but the truth is I'm not going to leave a positive review for a game I didn't enjoy playing. And I think the community around this game has a bit of elitism around its high difficulty, and it blinds them to real flaws.

This is an old game so perhaps it's a bit silly to post a review for it at all, but I'd always heard good things about it and was excited to try it since I enjoy challenging strategy games and dark fantasy settings. It's not really much of a strategy game though. Each character has access to only a small number of moves, of which 1-2 are phenomenally powerful and good in almost all circumstances, and another 1-2 are situationally useful, and the rest are garbage. The list is further cut down by only being able to use certain abilities when standing in a certain rank of your party and against a certain rank of the enemy party. The upshot is that on any given turn, each character tends to have exactly 1 move which is the no-brainer choice. And it's pretty much always the exact same kind of move that's good in other similar strategy games. Use stuns whenever possible, use DoTs in long fights, stall at the end of each fight and grind out some heals of health and stress, etc. Very repetitive and tactically trivial gameplay. But also, there is a huge amount of luck and randomness. Dice are rolled to determine what dice are rolled to determine what dice are rolled to determine what options you have. (E.g. you get random heroes who have random starting skills, your heroes might randomly not be available for a given mission because they're off on a bender, then your encounter chance is random, and then there's a random chance that you're surprised or the enemy is, and then it's random
A bit too many mechanics for my taste. I'm still in the tutorial after an hour

I have tried several times before to get into Darkest Dungeon; I really want to like it because the art style and the music and the narration are all so good. Unfortunately Darkest Dungeon is complete anti-fun as a game. The combat is frustrating and the town management is tedious. Basing your game around super punishing RNG is just so terrible. In a difficult RPG with little to no RNG such as a Souls-like, I know that success comes down to my ability to form a plan and execute it competently. In an RNG heavy game like Darkest Dungeon, I can pick what are ostensibly the correct choices only for the computer to tell me 'nah, get ♥♥♥♥♥♥' and throw a run directly into the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. This instantly kills my motivation to keep playing. Hell, I'll even start a save on the baby difficulty with some workshop mods to balance things in my favor and I still can't get past like 7-8 expeditions before I reach that point of staring at the town screen, scrolling through my character roster with glazed-over eyes, and then saying '♥♥♥♥ this' before uninstalling. I love the idea of Darkest Dungeon but man I just cannot stand playing it.

Honestly, it's just not that fun. There's generally some aspect of RNG management in healthy turn-based combat systems- there's even nothing inherently wrong with one that centralizes this either, but needs a healthy balancing of other systems to keep it meaningfully engaging and not simply frustrating. I feel the game considerably fails in this regard- RNG is extreme and punishing and you are given virtually zero tools to mitigate this; some of the tools you have are themselves subject to randomly being unavailable. This could still make for a fun game, constantly requiring you to "play it where it lands," and think on your feet, a little counterintuitive given the traditional RPG appeal of preparation over reactivity, but surely has plenty of its own depth to plumb regarding strategies resistant to the chaos and getting better at steering oneself out of dire straits. This game at its best succeeds at capturing this, though somewhat hamfistedly, the game always feels like a patchwork of systems that don't quite fit with one another. But where this game REALLY fails, it is EXTREMELY PUNISHING- every major failure can set you back hours of tedious, repetitive grinding, which in itself is subject to random failure, becoming this tired matryoshka of meaningless ♥♥♥♥ and frustration. The game fundamentally does not respect your time, which is sad, because even the RNG heavy systems are clearly capable of being mastered- I just have no interest in a learning curve that's mostly in

This game is unreasonable, unpredictable, and mostly un-fun.

AtO is one of the most unique multiplayer deckbuilders out there, with lots of interesting elements, build options, different activities like dailies and other challenges, and plenty of character/role diversity as well. In theory, virtually any comp can clear the game at its higher difficulties with proper planning and, well, some luck at certain points, but pretty much all the time you could say that your losses are your own for a variety of reasons, not just bad luck. The game is a roguelite, to start, so it is absolutely filled with meta progression. You'll have to get your 50 perk points before you can really begin aiming for solid builds in all of your runs, and at higher difficulties the different places you can freely assign those points shrinks more and more, as viable perk setups begin to narrow. That being said, there is a lot of fun in making off-comps work. With enough skill and planning, you can certainly make any team of characters succeed, and it's not overwhelming at all if you have a friend or a few so you're each playing one deck instead of playing four decks alone. The gameplay revolves entirely around buff and debuff stacking, however. Just making your gear and cards better and hoping to kill with straight DPS doesn't work, though it's obviously a core part of the game. Got a lot of time out of this game before the development team changed. Truly enjoyed this when it first came out as it created a fun premise my friends and I enjoyed. I didn't just recommend this game, I regularly bought friends copies so I could play it with them. It was unique in its initial execution, allowing you to strategize with your friends, build around each other, and feel powerful with fun cards, buffs, and interactions. Very unique mechanics for a turn-based multiplayer game. Unfortunately, some aspects of it haven't aged particularly well. Slay the Spire 2 allowing everyone to act within the same turn makes multiplayer combat feel dramatically faster and more natural by comparison. A lax run of Across the Obelisk can take several hours with friends, while our comparable Slay the Spire 2 runs tend to be significantly shorter. That doesn't suddenly make Across the Obelisk bad, but it does make how slow and precise every individual turn can be much more noticeable now. End of initial review. This repetitive game is impossible to fully complete without playing for hundreds of hours... And yet it offers less than 2 hours of actual content (around 20 enemies, 3 acts +1), that you can go through with 4 different characters (each one with a different set of cards) - which already means doing the same thing 4 times, imho. Seems fun to play during the first few hours, then it becomes a chore when you have to play the same content again and again, ad nauseam. But there's worse... The challenge in this game isn't fighting enemies, but rather building a good deck despite the game's crippling way of handling random loot. A deck-builder? No, that’s not what this game is. Trying to build a deck in a specific way is actually a good way to lose. In reality, this game is a battle against RNG. When you give players random rewards (e.g. boss fight rewards), you can make sure they always get at least a certain number of decent rewards during their run... but not here. Sometimes there are some good rewards, sometimes there are none. Sometimes a run is incredibly easy, sometimes winning is just impossible. Full random. This is NOT a balanced game... And if RNG ruins your run, too bad... You'll just have to start everything over and waste another hour trying to fight the RNG again. In a game that is already asking you to replay the same content an infinite number of times, this is not a good design.

These kinds of game are the equivalent to a certain generation of gamer's slots machine. Once you come to understand the mechanics, success/failure comes down to pulling the lever a certain number of times for the game to say "jackpot". The game tricks you into thinking there's deeper gameplay when you don't understand the game, however once you do understand it, you realize it's mostly RNG. Many faults in the mechanics: not being able to hold onto cards so that you can build a strategy to exploit the synergy of the cards you have in your deck, not being able to compound energy so you can take actions, many many other faults, all have ways to fix them, but it's random whether or not you will come across them in any particular run. Even even if you do, it's random whether or not it will be at a point where it will even matter.
